summary:
**SPHEREx Blink**

Every six months, SPHEREx photographs the entire sky in infrared. Somewhere in those billions of pixels, a brown dwarf is drifting and a nearby star is creeping across the field. No one can flip through that many images by hand, so we built a tool that flips through them for you.

Type a name or coordinates into SPHEREx Blink. It finds every SPHEREx visit to that spot, cuts out a small window and plays the visits like a flipbook. Switch to difference view and anything that moved shows up as a dark-and-bright pair. Overlay Gaia stars to tell the fixed from the wanderers, check for NEOSSat coverage, or measure the target's spectrum. Each frame shows its date and wavelength, because SPHEREx sees the same spot in different colors on each pass. Any view can be shared as a link.

It matters because discovery shouldn't need a PhD or terabytes of downloads. A curious student can watch a nearby star shift position in seconds, and might spot the next surprise.

That's about 190 words. I left comets and asteroids out on purpose, because that mode isn't working yet (the two presets have the wrong coordinates). If you fix it before submitting, add one line about tracking solar-system objects.
details:
SPHEREx Blink turns NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky survey into a flipbook for any spot on the sky. Type a star name or coordinates, press play, and every SPHEREx image of that spot flips past, lined up north-up. Anything that moved or changed brightness between visits jumps out.

Try it: https://spherexblink.vercel.app (it opens on WISE 0855-0714, the coldest known brown dwarf, crawling across the frame)

WHY WE BUILT IT

- Blinking between photos of the same sky found Pluto in 1930. Backyard Worlds volunteers used the same trick to find more than 3,000 brown dwarfs in NASA's WISE images.

- NEOWISE switched off in 2024. SPHEREx now photographs the whole sky every 6 months in 102 colours (0.75–5 µm), which makes it the obvious next survey to blink.

- Blinking SPHEREx, though, meant 65.7 MB files, an archive query language and FITS headers. Nobody had built a WiseView for SPHEREx, so we did: no code, no downloads, just a browser.

WHAT YOU CAN DO WITH IT

1. Search any name or RA/Dec, or pick one of 8 demo targets.

2. Flip through one stacked image per visit, a difference view, every single exposure (by date or by wavelength), or a view with the static sky removed.

3. Switch between the 6 detectors and fields from 3′ to 20′. Zoom, pan, and A/B blink two frames.

4. Measure the target's motion across the sky, and get its 0.75–5 µm spectrum as a CSV.

5. Overlay Gaia DR3 stars (ESA) and see NEOSSat observations of the same field (CSA, via CADC).

6. Share a link that reopens the exact view, embed the player, or export a WebM clip.

HOW IT WORKS

- Search: one ADQL query to NASA/IPAC IRSA finds every Level 2 image (DR1 plus the weekly QR3 release) that covers the position, so new data shows up within a day.

- Read only what's needed: HTTP range requests pull just the headers, the rows around the target, the quality-flag rows and the wavelength table. For a 3′ field that's 368 KB of each 65.7 MB file, about 0.6%.

- Process: subtract the background, reproject each cutout with its own WCS onto one north-up grid, and stack each visit with inverse-variance weights and 3σ clipping. Fast movers are centred on where they are in 2026.

RESULTS ON REAL SPHEREx DATA

- WISE 0855-0714: we measure 7.9 ± 1.0″/yr. The catalogue value is 8.1″/yr.

- Barnard's Star: 8.9 ± 1.2″/yr against a catalogue 10.4″/yr. It saturates the detector, so we locate it from its blanked-out core.

- Epsilon Indi B: 247 clean spectrum points over 4 visits show a deep methane dip near 3.3 µm, the signature of a cold brown dwarf rather than a star.

- With 3 visits over one year, about 1″/yr is the honest precision.

WHAT'S NEW

SPHEREx's filters change wavelength across each detector, so every exposure sees the target in a slightly different colour. We turn the flipbook itself into a spectrum. And because we read bytes instead of whole files, the tool runs for free on one serverless function.

IMPACT

Students, amateur astronomers and citizen scientists can search SPHEREx for nearby brown dwarfs, variable stars and moving objects the way volunteers searched WISE. Every new SPHEREx pass makes each flipbook longer and more sensitive. That is what a search for Planet X needs: something faint that moves.

BUILT WITH

Python (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, PyVO), TypeScript (React, Vite, HTML canvas), hosted on Vercel.
